_note: Plain-English glosses for the jargon on this site. Written by hand, not generated: a model that invents definitions would be the one thing here you could not check. Each entry carries the domain and shape tags that Cypha uses as its feature vector — see assets/js/glossary.js.

terms.g: When a program can do anything you can do, just because it is running as you. It is why one compromised app can read every file you own.
A key handed to a program for one specific thing. No key, no access — so a program can only touch what it was given, not everything you own.
The small core of the system that hands out those keys and refuses every request that does not carry one.
Stopping a program from reading or writing memory it was never given. Roughly two in three serious security holes are this one mistake.
A program keeps using a piece of memory after handing it back. Someone else gets that memory, and now they can see or change what the program is doing.
Writing more data than the space set aside for it, so the extra spills into whatever sat next door. A classic way to take over a program.
A version of the FreeBSD operating system with extra defences built in. ParanoidBSD starts from it rather than from scratch.
A free, open-source operating system, related to the one inside macOS. Widely used in network hardware and servers.
The part of an operating system with total control of the machine. Everything else asks it for permission.
How a normal program asks the kernel to do something it cannot do itself, like open a file or send data.
Code that runs with no operating system underneath it, so it cannot rely on the usual conveniences. The kernel has to be written this way.
The agreed rules two pieces of compiled code follow so they can call each other without knowing each other's source.
The 2023 version of the C++ language. It can express who owns a piece of memory, which older C cannot.
A rule that memory is never writable and runnable at the same moment, so an attacker cannot write in new instructions and then run them.
Shuffling where things sit in memory each run, so an attacker cannot guess the address they need.
A FreeBSD feature that lets a program voluntarily give up most of its own powers before handling risky input.
Tools that run a program and shout when it touches memory it should not, or does something the language leaves undefined.
Run the old version and the new version on the same input and compare. If they disagree anywhere, the new one is wrong.
The halfway form a compiler turns code into before producing machine instructions. Comparing two programs here catches differences the source hides.
A written record of where each piece came from and how it was checked — so you can prove what is in the thing you shipped.
The design behind almost every well-known AI today, including ChatGPT. Powerful, but large and expensive to run.
The trick inside a transformer that lets every word look at every other word. It is also why the cost grows so fast with length.
A model that sorts things into groups — spam or not, faulty or fine.
A model that predicts a number rather than a category, like a price or a score.
A model that keeps learning from each new example as it arrives, instead of being trained once and frozen.
The compressed internal description a model builds — the handful of numbers it thinks actually matter.
Training a small model to copy a big one's answers, so you get most of the behaviour at a fraction of the size.
Data deliberately kept away from training, used to check the model learned something real rather than memorising.
A way of re-describing data so a simple straight-line model can separate patterns that are not straight lines.
The idea that a good model keeps only what is useful for the answer and throws the rest away.
The principle that the best explanation is the shortest one that still fits the evidence.
A theoretical description of the most capable possible learner. Impossible to build, useful as a yardstick.
A theory that intelligent things act to reduce their own surprise about the world.
A score for how surprised a language model is by real text. Lower is better; very high means it has not learned much.
The chemistry that makes stripes on animals and spots on shells — two substances spreading and reacting. Cell AI uses it instead of attention.
Learning rules copied from real brain cells: connections that fire together strengthen.
Takes a finished program, which is unreadable to people, and works backwards toward something you can read.
A rough, readable sketch of what code does. Useful, but it still does not tell you what the program is for.
The shipped, machine-readable form of a program — the thing you run when the source code is not included.
How a program packs data into a file or a message so it can be stored or sent, then unpacked later.
Several things happening at once inside one program. It is where the hardest and least repeatable bugs live.
Everything about a message except its contents: who, to whom, when, how big. Often more revealing than the message.
Working out what is going on purely from the pattern of messages, without ever reading one.
A relay network that shuffles and delays messages so an observer cannot match what went in to what came out.
Sending at a steady rate whether or not you have anything to say, so silence and conversation look identical from outside.
The worst realistic eavesdropper: someone who can see every link in the network at once but does not tamper with it.
A model for events that trigger more events — one burglary raising the odds of the next one nearby.
The standard model for events that happen at random with no memory. Useful as the boring baseline to beat.
A method that finds dense clumps in data and labels the leftovers as noise, without being told how many clumps to expect.
Turning scattered points into a smooth heat map, so you can see where things concentrate.
Working backwards from where a series of crimes happened toward where the offender probably lives.
The standard building blocks for matrix arithmetic that almost all scientific software sits on top of.
Standard ways of splitting a matrix into simpler pieces so equations can be solved quickly and accurately.
A decomposition that reveals the strongest patterns in a table of numbers. The maths behind a lot of data compression.
Finds the natural frequencies or directions of a system — how a bridge vibrates, how a network settles.
Equations describing how something changes over time or space. Heat spreading, a population growing, air over a wing.
Chopping a complicated shape into small simple pieces so a computer can work out the forces across it.
Software that does algebra the way a person does — with symbols — rather than only with numbers.
An open-source licence. Free to use and change, but if you build on it you must publish your changes too — including over a network.
You can read the code. Whether you can use it freely depends on the licence attached.
A desktop — windows, menus, settings — that runs on top of the operating system. The part you actually look at.
A toolkit for building desktop applications with normal windows and buttons.
Kickstarter's rule: if the goal is not reached by the deadline, nobody is charged and the project gets nothing.
